title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
text:
This is an interactive page covering the material from the SfN 2026 poster. Three of the figures are interactive — turn a cell type off in the legend and the rest redraw — and a few supplemental panels that did not fit on the board are included at the end of their section.
Download the original poster as printed (PDF, 5.6 MB)

title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
section: About the data in this poster
text:
About the data in this poster
Versions. The connectome is MICrONS minnie65_public. Every number on this page is at materialization v1926 unless it names another; v1300 is the state at the Nature 2025 release and is the baseline every “since publication” comparison uses.


1,355neurons in a 100 µm column153,178synapses between those neurons643,464connections from the column to any neuron1,384,465total unique connections in the 1 mm³ volume

title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
text:
01 — The MICrONS dataset

A volume electron-microscopy reconstruction of roughly a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex, spanning V1 and the higher visual areas lateral to it. Every object in the render is a segmented process from the automated segmentation; the colours are arbitrary and are there to separate neighbours, not to encode type.
This reconstruction is the substrate for everything below. The automated segmentation gets dendrites largely right but axons are often falsely-truncated or falsely-merged to other neurits. Section 02 describes the ongoing manual proofreading efforts to extend the axons.
The MICrONS Consortium et al., Nature 2025. doi:10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w

title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
text:
02 — Ongoing refinement
Proofreading is not a binary. A cell moves along a ladder — untouched, clean, partially extended, fully extended — and where it sits determines which questions it can answer. An unproofread axon is not a short axon; it is an axon whose reconstruction truncated early and often includes falsely-merged axon from another source. Counting its synapses gives an answer that is largely unpredictive of its corrected reconstruction.

Where the tracked population sits, and where it moved

Status at the Nature release (v1300) on the left, status now (v1926) on the right, for the V1 column and for the tracked cells outside it. The column is the campaign this poster is about: 1,355 cells, of which 541 are now fully extended (prioritized by the least proofread to extend first) and 813 partially. Outside the column the work is broader and shallower, and the interareal category — axons followed specifically across an area border — exists only there.
Read the thickness, not the endpoints: most of the movement is partially → fully extended, which is the expensive half of the ladder.


What fully extending one neuron takes










One cell, nucleus 296503, before and after. The dendrite (dark) was already correct; the light grey axon is what the segmentation and earlier cleanup provided, and the purple is what full extension added. Axon length goes 6.2 → 20.0 mm.
The right panel is the same cell against the clock. Output synapses rise from 659 to 2,484 over 69 hours of human work — and the curve is close to linear, meaning there is no easy plataeu at which we consider a cell representaitonally complete until it is complete within the volume.


Output synapses added, across the whole column

Every column neuron, grouped by type, sorted within type. Grey is what was there at the Nature release; the coloured bar is what proofreading added since. The deep types gained least in absolute terms because they had least axon in the volume to begin with — an L6CT axon leaves through the white matter — while L4 and L2/3 gained the most.

There are a total 1,834,067 logged manual edit operations — made by 152 people. This is an incredible effort that absolutely will not scale to larger connectomes. However, all of the edit information is released publicly as training data and informs model advances in autoproofreading.

title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
text:
03 — Direct our proofreading
The column effort is winding down; the proofreading effort is not. VORTEX takes requests for which cells to proofread next, from anyone with a question that needs a cleaner reconstruction than the automated segmentation gives.
Submit a VORTEX request → www.microns-explorer.org/vortex

title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
section: 04 — A cortical column, every neuron proofread
text:
04 — A cortical column, every neuron proofread
A 100 µm column through all layers of V1, in which every neuron has been proofread rather than a sample. That is what makes the analyses in section 05 possible: a connection that is absent is really absent, not merely untraced.

Every arbor in the column

All 1,168 excitatory neurons with a cell-type label, every dendrite and axon drawn in place and coloured by meso_type. Line width is Strahler order, so trunks read heavier than tips; dendrite is drawn 1.5× the axon’s width at the same order and the axon is the same hue darkened.
The somata occupy a patch about 130 µm across. The arbors span 1,425 µm. That gap is the whole argument for the next two sections: a column is a small object whose output is not.
The grey behind the soma panels is the untracked population — 132,224 of the volume’s 134,569 cells — binned by soma density.


Where the cells are, by type
The interactive version of the soma panels above. Click a type in the legend to hide it; double-click one to isolate it. Hover gives the depth and the nucleus id.




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Soma positions of every labelled cell in the column, depth against the medial–lateral axis. Excitatory types are circles, inhibitory families diamonds.

title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
section: 05 — What analysis does a dense column enable?
text:
05 — What analysis does a dense column enable?

Directed connectivity graph

Every connection between the labelled column cells: presynaptic down, postsynaptic across, grouped by type and ordered by soma depth within type, so the diagonal is the column’s depth axis. Mark size and ink both carry synapse count.
The structure you can read off it without counting anything: the inhibitory rows are dense with outputs and the inhibitory columns are dense with inputs across layers, basket and Martinotti most of all. There is a conspicuous column at L5ET, representing the dense inputs across layers. Excitatory-excitatory connectivity is sparse and most often 1 synapse per connections. Recurrent connections dominate in layers 2, 3, and 4. The numbers behind that texture are in the next figure.

This table is complete, not a sample. The column’s internal synapses were queried with both partners restricted to the column set, so a blank cell is a real absence rather than an untraced one. 82,614 connections, 152,336 synapses, 4.7% of ordered pairs connected. Of the pairs connected at all, 14.4% are reciprocal — six times what a random graph of this density gives.



Type to type, as proportions
The matrix as numbers. A dot’s area is the proportion of one type’s local synapses that the pair accounts for; the left panel normalises each row (of everything this type sends locally, where does it go) and the right normalises each column (of everything this type receives locally, where is it from).
Click a type in the legend to drop its row or column. Hover gives the synapse count and both denominators.




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Type-to-type connectivity as proportions of local synapses. Top: each row sums to 1 across that type’s local output. Bottom: each column sums to 1 across that type’s local input. One size scale across both panels.






excitatory -> interneurons : 29–58% of local output
basket + Martinotti -> each excitatory type : 41–71% of local input
local share of output : excitatory 10.0%, inhibitory 19.0%
local share of input  : excitatory 3.1%, inhibitory 4.2%


Three things the two panels say together:

Local excitatory output is mostly inhibitory recruitment. Every excitatory type sends between 29% and 58% of its local output to interneurons — L6CT puts 41% into Martinotti cells alone.
Each type’s heaviest excitatory target sits near its own depth. L6CT sends 29% of its local output to L6CT and 1.0% to L2IT. The diagonal of the excitatory block is the column’s depth axis.
Input is inhibition-dominated everywhere. Basket plus Martinotti supply between 41% and 71% of every excitatory type’s local input.


“Local” is carrying all three of those. Every proportion is of the synapses inside the column, and that is a small and uneven slice: excitatory cells place 10.0% of their output inside the column and receive 3.1% of their input from it; inhibitory cells 19.0% and 4.2%. So an inhibitory row is a proportion of twice as large a slice as an excitatory one. The reason is section 06 — excitatory axons leave, inhibitory axons largely do not.



Not on the poster: type-to-type as a static figure

The print version of the interactive figure above, with the denominators written beside each row and above each column.


Modest expansion reveals reciprocal motifs

The column’s cells were proofread first; the expanded ring of interneurons around them came later. Adding 213 inhibitory cells to the 160 already tracked takes basket ↔︎ 5P-IT reciprocal pairs from 52 to 134.

That is not proofreading finding more synapses within the core column. Of the 82 extra pairs, 76 required a cell that was not in the core set at all and only 6 are new links between cells that were already there. The series is a statement about how much more of the circuit is visible with modest expansion, a nonlinear payoff for effort, not about the circuit itself.



Functional unit, with coregistration

A coregistered cell is one matched to the two-photon imaging, so a coreg → coreg connection is the unit a structure–function analysis can use. The coregistered population does not change between versions — 15,439 cells at both v1300 and v1926 — so nothing here is relabelling, only an increase in proofread connections
336 coregistered column cells gained more than five output synapses between the versions. Those cells put 28,844 new connections onto 10,498 recipients, binned here at the recipient rather than the source. 336 cells in a 130 µm patch reach most of a 1,160 µm sheet.


Not on the poster: the column from above

The dashed box is the EM volume. The volume is about 1,250 µm medial-to-lateral and only about 530 µm anterior-to-posterior, so the cloud reaching the top and bottom edges is the edge of the tissue, not the arbors naturally terminating. Whereas many arbors naturally terminate in the lateral dimension, as seen in 06.

title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
text:
06 — Interareal connections

Column axons that reach a higher visual area

The volume spans the V1 border, so a column axon that projects to a higher visual area can be followed into it. Grey is cable that stays in V1; coloured cable has crossed the boundary at 1,054 µm into VISrl.
Beneath, the same cells’ output synapses as a density along the medial–lateral axis. The distal bump is not a shoulder of the local peak: it is a patch, 132 µm past the boundary, and 85% of the distal output falls within 225 µm of it.

“Retinotopically matched” is approximate as measured from the in vivo retinotopic sign-mapping. The precise position of that patch is drawn by this figure as the natural reading of the axon projections.



How far the output goes, by type
The density curve above, split by the source cell’s type. Click a type in the legend to hide it.




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Output synapses per micrometre along the medial–lateral axis, by presynaptic type. The dashed line is the V1/VISrl boundary; everything to its right is interareal.






Layer 5 on its own

Layer 5 — ET, IT and NP together — crosses the boundary more often than the column as a whole: 91 of 135 cells (67%) against 560 of 1,168 (48%). But it places a smaller share of its synapses past the line, 5.6% against 6.6%. More L5 cells reach the higher area; each one puts less there.

title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
text:
07 — Connectome in context

The same volume holds the non-neuronal cells, densely segmented along with the neurons. A set of astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia within the column have undergone proofreading to clean and complete their processes. On the left an oligodendrocyte, with an inset from the EM imagery showing myelin wrapped around the axon it ensheathes. On the right a microglial cell, with every synapse within 500 nm of its processes marked — 4,648 of them.
Neither is part of the connectome as usually defined, but here the non-neuronal cells are in the same reconstruction with the neurons they support and synapses they modify.

Also in the column: 126 astrocytes
On the printed board this render sits in block 04, beside the neurons it was reconstructed alongside. It belongs here, with the rest of the glia.

Every astrocyte whose soma falls in the column, 126 of them, each a separate colour. Click to open it larger — even then the cells read as territories rather than as individual arbors; the single astrocyte in block 04’s gallery is the one to look at for morphology.
Two things come out of seeing the population rather than one cell. The territories read as discrete — each astrocyte a patch of colour meeting its neighbours rather than mixing through them — which is what astrocyte tiling looks like, though nothing here measures the overlap. And the stack carries the same rightward kink as the neuronal column in block 04, because it is the same piece of tissue: the column is defined on the neurons, and the astrocytes inside it inherit its shape.

title: Insights from a visual cortical column connectome
text:
08 — Organelle segmentation

The resolution required for segmenting synapses also yields segmentable organelles, such as mitochondria. Here, mitochondria inside one neuron, each as a separate object.

Mitochondrial content differs between excitatory and inhibitory cells and between compartments, in every measure: mean mitochondrion size, the fraction of compartment volume they occupy, their number per micrometre of axon, and their number per output synapse. Inhibitory axons carry more and larger mitochondria than excitatory axons. However excitatory dendrites show larger and more numerous mitochondria. This is especially apparent in large apical dendrites.
These results are from a 40 x 40 x 80 um test volume provided by Constantin Pape et al. Full-volume segmentation is in progress.
